title: V3-7 — Coastal Process Science: Why Beaches Move
summary: A beach is not a place, it's a flow: sand rivers along the shore (longshore transport), the profile breathes on-offshore with storms and calms, and grain size is destiny. A groin is a wall across the sand river — with a guilty secret downstream. PLAIN: sand is always moving; you're managing a current, not placing a carpet. PRO: littoral drift, sediment budgets, equilibrium profiles, pre-filled groin fields, the baseline survey that's legally priceless.

sections.heading: The sand river
sections.body: PLAIN: Waves almost never arrive straight-on — they hit at a slight angle, push sand up the beach at that angle, and gravity drags it straight back. Every wave moves each grain a small zigzag step sideways; millions of waves make a slow river of sand flowing along the shore. A beach that 'stays put' is a checkbook that balances: sand arriving equals sand leaving. Your rocky Yamacraw shoreline is rocky BECAUSE its checkbook runs a permanent deficit — you're not building a beach, you're depositing a large balance (fill) and slowing the withdrawals (groins). PRO: 'littoral drift,' 'sediment budget,' 'net vs gross transport,' 'erosive shoreline — negative budget.'

sections.heading: What a groin does, and its guilty secret
sections.body: PLAIN: A groin is a wall across the sand river: sand piles up on the upstream side (success!) and the downstream side STARVES, because the river past the wall carries less while the waves keep withdrawing. Groins don't create sand — they redistribute your fill and everyone's drift. So the design answer is a groin FIELD (several, spaced so each compartment holds a stable pocket), PRE-FILLED with imported sand (so your groins trap your sand, not the neighbors'), tapered at the downdrift end — and the neighbor beyond your last groin is either a monitoring-and-mitigation commitment or a plaintiff. Palm Cay's half-moon pocket coves are this logic in built form. PRO: 'downdrift starvation,' 'pre-fill the groin field,' 'terminal groin taper,' 'headland breakwater / pocket beach,' 'equilibrium shoreline orientation'; field spacing ≈ 2–4× groin length, engineer's model governs.

sections.heading: The breathing profile, grain size, and the long game
sections.body: PLAIN: Beaches also move on-offshore: storms cut the dry beach down and drag sand to an offshore bar (it looks destroyed); calm long waves push much of it back by themselves. A beach has a preferred underwater shape — dump fill steeper than that shape and the sea re-grades it immediately, so the dry beach 'shrinks' alarmingly in year one even though the sand only moved underwater. Owners panic; you won't, because the monitoring surveys measure the whole profile, not the dry width. Grain size is destiny: coarser sand stands steeper and stays; finer flattens and flees — the physics behind M5's non-negotiable sand spec. Sea level rises slowly; on a flat carbonate island small vertical = large horizontal, so finished floors, seawall caps, and marina decks carry freeboard margin. PRO: 'storm bar / recovery,' 'equilibrium (Dean) profile,' 'profile adjustment losses year one' (10–25% of dry-beach APPEARANCE), 'design width vs advanced-fill width,' 'overfill ratio' 1.1–1.5× (extra fill because some loss is designed-in, not failure), 'freeboard for SLR over the design life.'

quiz.teach: The zigzag mechanism: angled wave up, gravity straight back down.
quiz.prompt: Explain why sand flows ALONG the shore rather than just in and out.

choices.text: Waves arrive at a slight angle and push sand diagonally up the beach; the backwash drains straight down the slope — each wave nets a small sideways step, and millions of waves make a river of sand along the coast
choices.why: Correct — the zigzag walk. That river (littoral drift) is what groins interrupt and sediment budgets account for.

choices.text: Ocean currents drag the sand parallel to shore
choices.why: Offshore currents matter far out; in the surf zone where beaches live, the ANGLED-WAVE zigzag dominates the transport.

choices.text: Wind blows the dry sand along the beach
choices.why: Aeolian transport reshapes dunes; the volumetric river runs in the water, wave by wave.

choices.text: It doesn't — sand only moves in and out
choices.why: Cross-shore movement is real (the breathing profile) but the LONGSHORE river is why downdrift neighbors exist as a concept — and as plaintiffs.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: every wave nudges every grain a tiny step sideways — add up a year of waves and the beach is a conveyor. PRO: 'longshore transport / littoral drift; net vs gross; the sediment budget is the beach.' (V3-7)

quiz.teach: Pre-filling a groin field means importing the sand your groins will trap.
quiz.prompt: Why must the groin field be PRE-FILLED with imported sand rather than left to 'fill naturally'?

choices.text: An empty groin field fills by starving the drift — i.e., by eating the downdrift neighbors' beach; pre-filling means your compartments start full and the river past your last groin keeps flowing at nearly its natural rate
choices.why: Correct. 'Fill naturally' is a euphemism for 'confiscate the neighbors' sand supply' — the exact downdrift starvation that turns adjacent HOAs into plaintiffs.

choices.text: Natural filling is too slow for marketing
choices.why: It IS slow — but the disqualifying problem is WHOSE sand does the filling. The speed issue is commercial; the source issue is legal and physical.

choices.text: Pre-filling makes the groins structurally stronger
choices.why: Sand against a groin changes loading marginally; the pre-fill logic is sediment-budget ethics, not structural.

choices.text: DEPP requires it as a permit formality
choices.why: DEPP requires it BECAUSE of the downdrift physics — the regulation encodes the mechanism; it isn't arbitrary paperwork.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: build the trap already full, so it doesn't have to rob anyone to fill itself. PRO: 'pre-fill the compartments to design volume with the overfill ratio (1.1–1.5×); taper the terminal groin; monitor the downdrift baseline.' (V3-7, M5)

quiz.teach: Year-one 'losses' split into two very different categories.
quiz.prompt: Year-one survey: dry beach width down 25%, but total profile volume down only 6%. What do you tell the owners' meeting?

choices.text: Mostly good news, honestly delivered: the sea re-graded the fill to its equilibrium underwater shape — most of the 'lost' beach moved offshore within the profile, still yours, still doing its wave-energy job; the real loss (6%) is inside the designed-for overfill allowance
choices.why: Correct. Profile adjustment (10–25% of dry APPEARANCE in year one) is designed-in, which is why the overfill ratio existed. The whole-profile survey is what lets you say this with numbers instead of hope.

choices.text: Apologize — a quarter of the beach is gone
choices.why: The DRY WIDTH shrank; the SAND mostly didn't leave. Apologizing for equilibrium adjustment teaches owners to panic at physics — and undermines the real story the data tells.
Maybe partially true and entirely beside the point — the adjustment was predicted at design. Blaming weather for a designed-in process spends credibility you'll need for actual storm losses.

choices.text: Say nothing until year two's survey
choices.why: Owners watching their beach 'shrink' don't wait for data you're withholding — the first-news rule (M13) applies to physics too.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the beach didn't leave — it lay down. The sea reshaped the pile into its preferred underwater slope, and the survey proves the sand is still on the property. PRO: 'profile adjustment vs volumetric loss; design width vs advanced-fill width; the whole-profile monitoring is the answer to every dry-width panic.' (V3-7, M5)

mathProblems.title: The overfill order
mathProblems.context: The advanced-fill volume exceeds design volume by the overfill ratio — extra sand ordered because year-one adjustment loss is designed-in, not failure. Compute the EXTRA volume (ratio minus 1, as a percentage).

decisionPoints.title: Groin field or Palm Cay coves?
decisionPoints.scenario: The coastal engineer presents two beach architectures: (A) five groins + 120,000 cy of pre-fill — more continuous beach, higher downdrift interaction to model and monitor; (B) three headland breakwaters forming pocket coves, Palm Cay style — nearly self-contained sediment cells, calmer swimming, less total dry beach, different permit profile. Marketing wants maximum beach length; the neighbors' HOA will read the EIA's downdrift section with a lawyer.

options.label: Have the engineer score both on downdrift risk, swimmer experience, lifecycle cost (renourishment cycle differs), and permit friction — with the Palm Cay coves' actual storm performance (free full-scale modeling, ten minutes away) as evidence
options.outcome: The comparison usually narrows to: coves cost more per foot of beach but nearly eliminate the downdrift fight and renourish less often — on a site flanked by organized neighbors, that trade frequently wins. Either way, the decision is made on the four axes that matter, with a built precedent as data.

options.label: Take the groin field — marketing's beach-length number is the product
options.outcome: Defensible IF the downdrift modeling is bulletproof and the monitoring-and-mitigation commitment is funded — you've chosen the architecture with the most neighbors in it. The beach is longer; so is the EIA's most contested section.

options.label: Do both — groins on one reach, coves on another, without re-modeling the combined system
options.outcome: Coastal structures interact: the cove field changes the wave climate and sand supply the groin field sees. Mixing architectures un-modeled means neither behaves as designed — the shoreline is one system, not a menu.

decisionPoints.debrief: Beach architecture is a systems choice: groin fields buy length and downdrift obligations; pocket coves buy stability and permit peace at higher unit cost. Palm Cay's built coves on your exact wave climate are the cheapest model run you'll ever get — walk them after the next big swell. (V3-7, M5, Appendix C)
